summary: The Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) effort aims to complement ingress filtering with finer-grained, standardized IP source address validation. This document describes threats enabled by source address spoofing, reviews current solutions and challenges, and begins an analysis of host-level anti-spoofing work.

plainLanguage.summary: IP packets carry a source address that the network never checks, so a host can claim to be any address it likes. This RFC describes the attacks that follow and what local checks can catch them. The goal is protection a site can deploy on its own, not only filtering at the edge of the Internet.

questions: how do i detect spoofed ip addresses
how do i validate ip addresses on my network
subtitle: What spoofed IP source addresses let an attacker do, and what a site can check for itself.

tldr.problem: The IP layer keeps no record of which host sent a packet, so any host can put a false source address in its packets, and that ability is used for floods, hijacks and hiding.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes source address validation: checking a packet's source address against the address binding, topology and switch port it arrived on, and dropping the packet when they disagree. It surveys the existing tools, from BCP 38 ingress filtering to unicast reverse path forwarding and learned port bindings, and the topologies that make binding hard.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC that sets the threat scope for the SAVI work rather than specifying a mechanism. It is explicit that validation yields evidence, not proof, and that logging bindings has privacy costs the operator must manage.

facts.label: Hosts on one subnet in a campus LAN

today: RFC 6959 is an Informational RFC published in May 2013. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It sets out the threat scope for the SAVI work: what source address spoofing enables, what the available tools do, and where local deployment is hard.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol, both IPv4 and IPv6, forwards packets hop by hop with no connection state at the network layer. The network keeps no record of the hosts using it. That is usually a benefit, but it has one consequence: a host that generates a packet can put any source address it likes in it, because nothing in the network can tell that the address is false.

Source address validation is the check that detects and rejects such spoofed packets, and it contributes to the overall security of IP networks. This document covers the subset of validation the network does from observed traffic and policy. Such techniques let a network detect and reject many spoofed packets, and they implicitly give some assurance that the source address in a packet really was assigned to the system that sent it.

BCP 38 describes ingress filtering guidelines for this purpose. The weakness the RFC points at is deployment: unless the filtering happens at the ingress point of the network, the validity of the source address cannot be positively ascertained, and BCP 38 gives little benefit until it is very widely deployed, which it is not. SAVI aims to provide protection that a site can apply locally and that is locally useful, which gives the site a reason to deploy it while the Internet as a whole moves towards widespread BCP 38 deployment.

Local protection also buys traceability. When an enterprise is told that an attack came from one of its addresses, the staff want to trace that address back to the machine inside the enterprise that sent it. That needs two things: usable address assignment and usage information, which comes from logging, and accurate information from source address validation, which shows that no other machine could have been using that address. On a LAN where several hosts share one switch port, one of them can also spoof the source addresses of the others, which is why the RFC treats topology as part of the threat.
sections.plainLanguage: IP packets carry a source address that the network never checks, so a host can claim to be any address it likes. This RFC describes the attacks that follow and what local checks can catch them. The goal is protection a site can deploy on its own, not only filtering at the edge of the Internet.

sections.title: Terms Used in This Document
sections.content:
The RFC defines the terms it needs, and two of them carry most of the argument.

Spoofing is the act of sending a datagram whose contents at the link layer or network layer do not match the network policies and activities around address assignment or claiming. In practice it means sending messages with source network or link-layer information that is assigned to, or properly claimed by, some other device in the network.

The binding anchor is the relationship a device performing source address enforcement uses to do the validation and enforcement. Examples in different situations include Layer 2 addresses or physical ports. The RFC also names the network elements it discusses: the CPE router on the customer premises, the PE router that faces a customer of a provider, and the NNI router that faces a system operated by another provider.
sections.plainLanguage: Two terms matter most. Spoofing means sending a packet with a source address that belongs to someone else. A binding anchor is the link between an address and something physical, such as a switch port or a hardware address, that the network can check against.

sections.title: Spoof-Based Attack Vectors
sections.content:
Spoofing is used on the Internet mostly for malicious purposes. The RFC splits the attacks into two classes. Blind attacks happen when the attacker is not on the same local area network as the source or the target and has no access to the data path between them. Non-blind attacks involve an attacker who can see the traffic, such as a man in the middle.

Among the blind attacks, a single packet can crash a target or poison its configuration. A LAND attack sends a packet, for example a TCP SYN, whose source and destination addresses are both the target's and whose source and destination port are the same. Some systems lock up when they build connection state for it, or reply to themselves indefinitely. The RFC notes that this attack relies on bugs in the target, so it may no longer be viable. A RST probe targets a long-lived TCP session: the attacker knows the addresses and ports and guesses the sequence number, and a close enough guess terminates the connection.

Flood-based denial of service floods the target with packets to exhaust its connection state, its processing capacity or its bandwidth. Because no reply is needed and no legitimate transaction state is created, the attacker often spoofs the source address to hide where the traffic comes from. The common forms named are SYN floods, ICMP floods and IP fragmentation attacks. Poisoning attacks corrupt cached information instead: an on-link attacker can poison a router's ARP or Neighbor Discovery cache, or a DNS cache, and a stream of packets may be used where one packet is not enough. Self-propagating malware has been observed spoofing its source address while spreading.

Reflective amplification attacks use a false source address so that an intermediary answers the target instead of the attacker. Against the DNS root and other top-level name server infrastructure in early 2006, the observed amplification factor was on the order of 72:1, so 27 attacking sources with 512 kbps of upstream attack bandwidth could generate 1 Gbps of response attack traffic towards a target. Smurf attacks work the same way against IP subnet broadcast addresses, and have been particularly effective in large campus LAN environments where 50K or more hosts share one subnet.

The non-blind attacks use the same capability for different ends. A man in the middle usually needs to be in the forwarding path, and in IPv4 it can get there by sending gratuitous ARP messages or ARP replies to the Ethernet broadcast address, telling every host on the segment that the target's IP address now maps to its own Layer 2 address. The source IP address in that case is spoofed. The same vulnerability exists in the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery protocol, although the multicast requirements of that protocol make it harder to exploit in the same generality. Third-party reconnaissance sends spoofed TCP SYN packets from a large set of source addresses and observes the responses, which reveals what IP-layer filtering policies protect the target.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC splits spoofing attacks into two kinds. Blind attacks need no reply, such as floods or a packet that crashes the target. Non-blind attacks need to watch the traffic, such as redirecting a session through the attacker.

sections.title: Current Anti-Spoofing Solutions
sections.content:
The goal is to reduce the number of datagrams with spoofed IP addresses arriving from the Internet. The tool is to identify and drop datagrams whose source address binding is incompatible with the network topology and with what has been learned about address assignment. Where the relationship between source address, topology and binding can be checked, the network can confirm that the IP source address matches the lower-layer address, that the source address is the one expected for the Layer 2 switch port the datagram arrived on, or at least that the prefix the address belongs to is right for that part of the network.

The primary action is checking the source IP address in the IP header. To support that, the addresses claimed in the messages that make such claims, such as ARP requests and responses, DHCP replies and IPv6 duplicate address detection messages, must also be examined and verified. SAVI is not concerned with addresses inside arbitrary higher-level protocol messages.

How much a check can be trusted falls off with distance from the source. The RFC lists the enforcement points in order of confidence: on the link to the source host, where both the link-layer and the IP address are known and can be compared, and on a switched link the source host can even be identified by the port the datagram arrived on; on upstream switches, where the state may have to move when the bridging topology, link aggregation or redundancy changes; on upstream routers, which cannot see the link-layer address and can therefore only confirm that the source address falls in an appropriate prefix; at the provider edge router, where enforcement depends on how much the provider trusts the downstream network; and between providers at the NNI, where unicast reverse path forwarding is less effective because of asymmetric routing. Cable modem and DSL access have their own points, and for DSL, enforcement can generally be done at the aggregation router, which sees which subscriber sent the packets.

Three tools are available today. BCP 38 filtering is typically applied on subnetwork boundaries, so hosts in a segment cannot spoof addresses from outside the segment but may still use addresses from inside it. Unicast reverse path forwarding automates BCP 38 style filters from the routing table. Port-based address binding is the main target of SAVI: binding an IP address to a port, to an unchangeable or authenticated MAC address, or to other credentials in the packet lets a switch reject an impostor. Binding information can be built by hand, but that does not scale with dynamic address assignment, so the RFC describes building it from the DHCP exchanges used for IPv4, from DHCPv6, or from the duplicate address detection messages that IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration uses.
sections.plainLanguage: The network checks the source address in the packet header and drops the packet when the address does not fit the place it came from. The closer the check is to the sending host, the more certain the answer. Switches can also learn which address belongs to which port from DHCP or IPv6 address claims.

sections.title: Topological Challenges Facing SAVI
sections.content:
Topology and the way addresses are handed out decide what a binding can be. Static configuration of access filters that map link-layer and network-layer addresses to a specific switch port can work in a strictly static environment, but most networks are dynamic, so a binding mechanism has to cope with DHCP, DHCPv6 and IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration.

Some devices are hard to bind to a port. Routers are the clearest case: they originate packets, often have several interfaces, and forward packets from other segments, so many addresses and subnets may legitimately belong to one port. NATs have the same problem, because they forward traffic from an array of addresses and validating them needs advance knowledge of which addresses belong to which port. Multi-instance hosts, such as blade servers or virtual machines sharing one switch port, add an internal switch of their own and may move between topologies while keeping their IP address, which forces the switches to update their state. Multi-interface hosts can send traffic with a loopback address or with the address of a third interface, and firewalls that forward packets or originate them locally behave like routers. Mobile IP hosts are not a problem, because their care-of address is properly assigned on the link they are using; a Mobile IP Home Agent is, because it forwards packets on behalf of other hosts.

IPv6 adds one more complication. SLAAC lets a host determine its prefix and choose an interface identifier without asking anyone, which makes behavioural enforcement harder because there is no control interaction. The 64-bit interface identifier space also lets a host mint anonymous addresses as often as it likes, and an on-link attacker may be able to generate enough addresses to fill the Neighbor Discovery table space of the other devices on the link, which would interfere with their ability to work.
sections.plainLanguage: Binding an address to a port is easy only for simple hosts. Routers, NATs, virtual machines and hosts with several interfaces all break the simple rule. IPv6 makes it harder again, because a host can pick its own addresses.

sections.title: What SAVI Can and Cannot Do
sections.content:
The RFC is careful about what source address validation can prove. It is tempting to think SAVI can trace a datagram to the person, or at least the end system, that sent it, but the technology gives circumstantial evidence only. Many systems have no user at all: middleware and application servers relay messages and perform services for users of other systems. And even if every network validated addresses at the ultimate network ingress, and intermediate devices were assured never to modify datagram source addresses, a source address still cannot be used as an authentication mechanism. The only techniques that unquestionably validate the source address of a received datagram are cryptographic authentication mechanisms such as IPsec.

Failure modes must be presumed in any SAVI deployment. An attacker inside the network may probe for the modes of spoofing that work, and if the probes stay below the alarm threshold the administrator learns nothing. Deployments have to be managed so that they do not give a false sense of security.

Enforcing and recording address bindings also has privacy implications, because binding data may count as personally identifying information. Prevention of spoofing does not by itself require keeping the logs: analysis of immediate events needs the current bindings, so removing binding logs once the binding lifetimes expire handles much of the problem, while logs of apparent spoof attempts are a separate matter and may need longer retention to detect patterns of deliberate or accidental abuse. If IPv6 SLAAC is used and IP to Layer 2 address bindings are logged, the administrator gains a way to associate users with their IP addresses even when IPv6 privacy addresses are in use.

Attribution also needs care. Whatever the theoretical strength of the tools, administrators should always allow for such information being wrong and should be careful about actions taken on the basis of apparent attribution. These techniques do nothing about address spoofing from other sites, so any evaluation of attribution has to allow for that too.
sections.plainLanguage: Address validation gives evidence, not proof. It cannot identify a person, and it is not a form of authentication. Logging the bindings also records where each user is, so the logs need a short life and careful handling.

items.title: LAND attack
items.text: A spoofed packet whose source and destination are the target makes some systems lock up.

items.title: RST probe
items.text: A guessed TCP sequence number resets a long-lived connection.

items.title: Flood-based DoS
items.text: Spoofed floods exhaust the target's state, processing or bandwidth.

items.title: Poisoning
items.text: Spoofed packets corrupt ARP, Neighbor Discovery or DNS cache entries.

items.title: Reflective amplification
items.text: A false source address makes an intermediary flood the target with replies.

items.title: Man in the middle
items.text: Spoofed ARP or Neighbor Discovery redirects traffic through the attacker.

items.title: Third-party recon
items.text: Spoofed probes reveal which filtering policies protect a target.

items.title: Accounting subversion
items.text: Spoofed sources hide content distribution from IP-layer accounting.
